builder_plan.scenario: Start with one repeated product task that has a measurable failure or cost.
builder_plan.change: Read the methods and identify one change you can isolate in that workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current implementation on the same held-out tasks.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful outcomes, response time, human rework, and total cost per successful task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Parallel Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics in Python: Task- and Data-Parallel SINDy with Numba, OpenMP, Threads and Multiprocessing for the Lorenz and Rössler Systems
summary: The method replaces PySINDy's interpreted library evaluation and least-squares solves with Numba-JIT loop kernels that accumulate normal equations in a cache-blocked pass, parallelized via prange, PyOMP, threads, or multiprocessing. It costs implementation and maintenance of custom compiled kernels plus a QR fallback path for ill-conditioned problems, and its 117x figure was measured on a 24-core dual-socket HPC node, not commodity hardware. It can fail numerically when normal equations are ill-conditioned (mitigated by the QR fallback) and the exact-coefficient guarantee is demonstrated only on the Lorenz and Rössler benchmarks, not on noisy or large-scale real data.
rationale: The paper accelerates sparse system identification on multicore CPUs, a scientific-computing workload unrelated to the reader's GPU/API-constrained ML production practice, so it does not warrant adoption or testing despite a strong quantified speedup.
technique: Parallel JIT-compiled SINDy with multiple CPU back ends

claims.statement: The method replaces PySINDy's interpreted library evaluation and least-squares solves with Numba-JIT loop kernels that accumulate normal equations in a cache-blocked pass, parallelized via prange, PyOMP, threads, or multiprocessing. It costs implementation and maintenance of custom compiled kernels plus a QR fallback path for ill-conditioned problems, and its 117x figure was measured on a 24-core dual-socket HPC node, not commodity hardware. It can fail numerically when normal equations are ill-conditioned (mitigated by the QR fallback) and the exact-coefficient guarantee is demonstrated only on the Lorenz and Rössler benchmarks, not on noisy or large-scale real data.

Compiled serial code is 4.3-5.6x faster than PySINDy; parallel back ends reach 14.8-20.3x speed-up on 24 cores (efficiency 0.61-0.84); overall time to solution reduced by up to 117x relative to PySINDy.
